name: Mato Grosso
summary_text: Mato Grosso stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and the 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism under constitutional and federal criminal provisions. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Entry, visa and gender-marker rules operate on the same footing for trans visitors as for anyone else, a position confirmed by an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 covering same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules nationwide.  Detention carries a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where arrested or imprisoned LGBTI people are housed. Recognition rests on self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. The place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a reasoned judicial decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Violence against trans and travesti people remains documented at national scale. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, released on 26 January 2026, records 80 murders of trans and travesti people across Brazil in 2025, 34 per cent below 2024, alongside at least 75 attempted homicides marked by excessive violence. Mato Grosso accounted for 3 of those killings in 2025, placing the state 12th among Brazilian states, and has recorded 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people since 2017.  Within Mato Grosso, a jury has explicitly recognised the gender dimension of a trans woman's killing. On 16 April 2026, businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, was sentenced to 13 years and six months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside the MT-485 highway in Sorriso, together with procedural fraud and corpse concealment. The jury held that the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.  The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.

name: Minas Gerais
summary_text: Minas Gerais is a state within Brazil and stands under the national framework set out for that country: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, an equal age of consent regardless of sexual orientation, and, since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions under which discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punished and transphobia is treated on the same footing as racism. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's documents and family-law status are handled the same as anyone else's at entry.  The dominant visitor-facing risk in Minas Gerais is lethal violence against trans people, and the state sits at the severe end of the national picture. The ANTRA dossier for 2024, published 27 January 2025, ranks Minas Gerais second nationally with 12 trans killings during the year, behind São Paulo with 16 and ahead of Ceará with 11. The cumulative count for the state across 2017 to 2024 is 100.  The following year's figures put the state at the head of the national ranking. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported on 26 January 2026, records Minas Gerais tied with Ceará in first place with 8 trans killings during 2025, within a national total of 80.  Detention in the state operates under a defined federal rule-set. A portaria issued on 17 April 2014 by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República sets housing rules for LGBT prisoners across Brazil's prison system and applies within the Minas Gerais state prison system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, together with the choice of male or female clothing.
